modules.summary: Use classic copywriting frameworks to structure persuasive messages, and support them with proof and objection handling.

lessons.title: AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action
lessons.body:
### A framework as old as advertising

**AIDA** — Attention, Interest, Desire, Action — describes the stages a reader moves through before acting. It dates back more than a century in sales and advertising, and it remains useful because it forces you to sequence your message rather than dumping everything at once.

### The four stages

| Stage | Reader's state | Copy's job | Techniques |
|---|---|---|---|
| Attention | Scrolling, distracted | Stop the right people | Specific headline, audience call-out, striking visual, pattern interrupt |
| Interest | Curious, not committed | Make them want to learn more | Relevant insight, problem framing, intriguing fact (true), story opening |
| Desire | Interested, weighing up | Make them want the outcome — and believe it | Benefits, outcomes, proof, vivid picture of success |
| Action | Ready or nearly ready | Make the next step clear and easy | Specific CTA, risk reversal, urgency if genuine |

### AIDA in a short social ad

```
ATTENTION: "Small online shop? Your abandoned carts are a goldmine."
INTEREST:  "Most shoppers who leave aren't saying no — they got distracted or had a question."
DESIRE:    "Our WhatsApp cart reminders answer questions and bring buyers back — shops using
            them recover sales they'd otherwise lose. (Results vary by store.)"
ACTION:    "Start a free 14-day trial ->"
```

### AIDA on a landing page

On a long page, AIDA maps to sections:

```
Attention  -> Headline + subheadline + hero visual
Interest   -> Problem section: "Sound familiar?" with 3 pains from research
Desire     -> How it works (3 steps), benefits, testimonials, case study, before/after
Action     -> Offer summary, guarantee, CTA; repeated CTA after FAQs
```

### Extending AIDA

Some marketers add stages:

- **AIDCA** — adds **Conviction** (proof and evidence) before Action, useful for sceptical or high-price purchases.
- **AIDAS** — adds **Satisfaction**, reminding you that post-purchase experience (onboarding, delivery) affects referrals and repeat purchases.

The names matter less than the idea: sequence the reader's journey, and do not ask for action before you have earned it.

### Step-by-step: writing with AIDA

1. **Define the reader and their awareness level.** A cold audience needs more Attention and Interest; a warm audience can move quickly to Desire and Action.
2. **Pick one message.** AIDA works best with a single core promise.
3. **Draft each stage separately** in a document with four headings.
4. **Check transitions.** Does each stage make the reader want the next?
5. **Cut.** Remove anything that does not move the reader forward.
6. **Check claims.** Every desire-building claim needs evidence.

### Worked example: a gym membership email

A gym in Manchester wants lapsed members to return in January.

```
Subject:   Your 2026 plan (without the January crowds)
ATTENTION: "You don't need a new-year resolution. You need a plan that fits your week."
INTEREST:  "Our coaches noticed most members who stop coming don't lose motivation —
            they lose their routine when life gets busy."
DESIRE:    "That's why we've built 30-minute express classes at 7 am, 12:30 pm and 6 pm,
            plus a free 15-minute plan session with a coach to fit training around your schedule.
            'I've kept going for six months because the times finally work.' — Priya, member"
ACTION:    "Book your free plan session — pick a time that suits you ->"
            "Your membership rejoin fee is waived until 31 January."
```

Note that the testimonial is genuine and used with permission, and the offer has a clear, real deadline.

### Before and after: AIDA applied to a WhatsApp broadcast

Many small businesses in Pakistan and the Gulf sell through WhatsApp Business broadcasts and catalogues. Messages are short, so AIDA has to be compressed — and messages may only go to people who opted in.

```
BEFORE
"Salam! New stock available. Check our page. Thanks"

AFTER
A  "Your winter wardrobe, sorted before the first cold week in Lahore."
I  "12 new unstitched khaddar suits just landed — the heavier fabric many of you asked for."
D  "Early buyers get free stitching on orders placed by Sunday (limit: first 40 orders)."
A  "Reply 1 to see the catalogue, or tap the link to order. Reply STOP to opt out."
```

Every stage is one line. The desire stage uses a genuine, bounded offer; the action stage gives two easy paths and a clear opt-out.

### Hands-on: AIDA as a structured prompt

When you use AI to draft, give the framework explicitly and ask it to label each stage — this makes the output easier to edit and to audit for invented claims:

```text
Write a [format, length] for [product] aimed at [audience, awareness level].
Use AIDA and label each part [A], [I], [D], [A].
Attention: use one of these verbatim customer phrases: [..].
Interest: explain how it works in 2 sentences.
Desire: use only these proof points: [..].
Action: CTA "[..]" plus one line of anxiety-reducing microcopy.
Do not add statistics, testimonials or claims not listed above.
```

Then delete the labels, read it aloud and edit for voice (see the editing and brand voice lessons).

### Measuring each stage

AIDA maps neatly onto metrics, which helps you diagnose which stage is weak:

| Stage | Signal that it is working (examples) |
|---|---|
| Attention | Hook rate / thumb-stop on video, open rate, headline click-through |
| Interest | Scroll depth, time on section, video watch-through |
| Desire | Clicks on pricing, add-to-cart, proof section engagement |
| Action | Conversion rate on the primary CTA, form completion |

If attention is strong but action is weak, rewriting the headline will not help — look at desire (proof, offer) and friction.

### Common mistakes

- Jumping straight to Action with cold audiences.
- Long Interest sections that never reach a point.
- Desire built on vague superlatives rather than outcomes and proof.
- Several different messages crammed into one AIDA sequence.
- Treating AIDA as rigid; sometimes Desire and proof are woven together.

### AIDA in video scripts

The framework works for short videos too. The first seconds are Attention (a visual or spoken hook), the next few seconds are Interest (the problem or insight), the middle is Desire (demonstration and proof), and the end is Action (a spoken and on-screen CTA). Because viewers can scroll away at any moment, compress Attention and Interest and show the product working as early as possible.

### AIDA planning template

```
Reader & awareness:
Core promise:
Attention (headline/hook):
Interest (problem/insight):
Desire (outcomes + proof):
Action (CTA + risk reversal + genuine urgency):
```
keyTakeaways: AIDA sequences a message: Attention, Interest, Desire, Action.
Cold audiences need more attention and interest; warm audiences can move faster to action.
Variants such as AIDCA add conviction for sceptical or high-price purchases.
Use one core message per AIDA sequence, supported by evidence.

knowledgeCheck.question: In AIDA, which stage uses testimonials, outcomes and a vivid picture of success?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Desire is where the reader comes to want and believe in the outcome.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the extra 'C' in AIDCA stand for?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Conviction adds proof and evidence before asking for action.

knowledgeCheck.question: A cold social audience sees an ad that opens with 'Buy now — 10% off'. What does AIDA suggest?
options: It skips attention, interest and desire that cold audiences need
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Cold audiences need to be earned before being asked to act.

knowledgeCheck.question: Your video ad has a strong hook rate and good watch time, but very few people click through or buy. Which AIDA stage should you investigate first?
options: Desire and action — proof, offer and friction
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Strong hook rate and watch time show attention and interest are working. The drop happens later, so look at the desire stage (proof, offer) and the action stage (CTA clarity and friction).

scenes.narration: Attention, interest, desire, action. Four words that have guided advertising for more than a century, and they still work on a TikTok video, a landing page and a WhatsApp broadcast. Why? Because they describe how a person moves from not caring to doing something. In this lecture you'll learn the four stages, how to write each one, how AIDA looks in a short social ad, a landing page and a video script, and how to measure which stage is failing. Then you'll watch me turn a flat WhatsApp message into a four-line AIDA broadcast.

scenes.narration: Why use a framework at all? Because a blank page is the enemy of good copy. Frameworks give you an order of operations, so you don't forget a step. The most common failure in amateur copy is skipping straight from attention to action. Look at this, buy now. The reader was never given a reason to care or a reason to believe. AIDA makes you slow down just enough to build interest and desire before you ask for anything. It's a checklist disguised as a story.

scenes.narration: Here's each stage. Attention: stop the right person, with a headline or hook that speaks to their situation. Interest: explain what this is and how it works, in terms they care about. Desire: make them want the outcome, with benefits, proof and the offer. Action: tell them exactly what to do next and remove the last worries. Think of it like a good first conversation at a networking event. You open with something relevant to them. You explain what you do in plain words. You share a result that makes them lean in. And you suggest a simple next step, like let's grab a coffee on Thursday.

scenes.narration: How does AIDA change by format? In a short social ad, each stage might be one line or a few seconds. In a landing page, each stage is a section: hero for attention, how it works for interest, benefits, testimonials and offer for desire, and a final CTA block for action. In a video script, attention is the first two seconds, often with on-screen text. Interest is the demonstration. Desire is the result and the proof. And action is a spoken and on-screen call to action. Same order, different lengths.

scenes.narration: A simple example: a gym membership email. Attention, the subject line: your first month, fifty percent off, this week only, but only if that's a genuine offer. Interest: the gym is a five-minute walk from your office, open from six a.m., with classes built for people who've never lifted before. Desire: members who come twice a week get a personalised plan and a check-in every month, and here's a short quote from a member, used with permission. Action: claim my first month, and underneath, cancel any time in the app. Four stages, one clear path.

scenes.narration: Let's also walk through AIDA on a landing page, section by section, because this is where most people use it. The hero is attention: a headline that names the outcome for a specific reader, and a subheadline that says how. Next comes interest: a short how it works section, three steps, with a screenshot or a short demo. Then desire, which is usually the longest part: benefits written as outcomes, testimonials placed next to the claims they support, and the offer with its guarantee. Finally action: a CTA block that repeats the primary button, answers the last two or three worries, and tells people exactly what happens after they click. If a section doesn't serve one of the four stages, ask whether it needs to be there at all.

scenes.narration: Here's where AIDA becomes a diagnostic tool. Each stage maps to a signal. Attention shows up in hook rate on video, open rate on email, and click-through on headlines. Interest shows up in scroll depth and watch time. Desire shows up in clicks on pricing, add-to-carts and engagement with the proof section. Action is the conversion rate on the primary CTA. So when a campaign underperforms, don't rewrite everything. Find the stage where people drop. If attention is strong but action is weak, a new headline won't help. Look at desire, meaning proof and offer, and at friction.

scenes.narration: A few extensions you'll hear about. Some writers add a stage for conviction, the proof that makes desire believable, between desire and action. Others add satisfaction or retention after action, the onboarding and follow-up that keep the customer happy. These are useful reminders, not rules. The core lesson stays the same. Earn each step before asking for the next one. And in video, AIDA often loops. A short clip might hook, demo, show the result, and then repeat a mini hook before the call to action, because viewers drift in and out.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Spending all your effort on attention and rushing the rest. Jumping from hook to buy now with no interest or desire. Using false urgency to force the action stage, like a deadline that isn't real. Writing desire with vague adjectives instead of outcomes and proof. And forgetting the action microcopy: what happens after I click, and can I change my mind? In messaging channels, one more: sending broadcasts to people who never opted in. That's not just bad AIDA. It can break the platform's rules and privacy law.

Write each stage on purpose, measure each stage separately, and fix the stage where people drop instead of rewriting everything. With AI, use AIDA as structure and supply your own proof. lessons.title: PAS and BAB: problem-led and transformation-led copy
lessons.body:
### Two frameworks for different moments

**AIDA** is general-purpose. Two other frameworks are especially powerful for short-form copy such as ads, emails and social posts:

- **PAS — Problem, Agitate, Solution**: starts with a pain the reader recognises.
- **BAB — Before, After, Bridge**: paints a transformation from the current state to a better one.

### PAS: problem, agitate, solution

```
PROBLEM:  Name a specific problem the reader has, in their words.
AGITATE:  Explore the consequences — why it matters, what it costs, how it feels.
SOLUTION: Present your product as the way out, with proof and a CTA.
```

Example for bookkeeping software:

```
PROBLEM:  "Every month-end, you're digging through WhatsApp for receipts."
AGITATE:  "Missing receipts mean missed expenses, a messy tax return, and another weekend lost
           to spreadsheets while clients wait for invoices."
SOLUTION: "Snap receipts as you go. Our app reads them, categorises them and gets your books
           ready for your accountant. Try it free for 14 days ->"
```

### Agitate responsibly

"Agitate" does not mean manipulate. It means helping the reader feel the real cost of the problem. Stay truthful and proportionate:

- Do not exaggerate risks or invent consequences.
- Be especially careful in sensitive categories — health, finance, children, body image — where advertising rules and platform policies are strict and fear-based messaging can cause harm.
- Never shame the reader. Empathy converts better and keeps your brand trusted.

### BAB: before, after, bridge

```
BEFORE: Describe the reader's current situation.
AFTER:  Describe life once the problem is solved.
BRIDGE: Show how your product gets them from before to after.
```

Example for an online Arabic course aimed at expatriates in the Gulf:

```
BEFORE: "You've lived in Dubai for three years and still switch to English the moment a
         conversation starts."
AFTER:  "Imagine chatting with your neighbours, reading menus and handling a taxi ride
         in Arabic — and seeing people's faces light up when you try."
BRIDGE: "Our 10-week conversational course uses real-life scenarios, 30-minute lessons and
         weekly speaking practice with native tutors. Book a free trial lesson ->"
```

### Choosing between frameworks

| Situation | Best fit | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Reader is problem-aware and frustrated | PAS | Starts where their attention already is |
| Reader is aspirational; product enables a positive change | BAB | Leads with the desired future |
| Longer page or email needing full journey | AIDA | Covers attention through action |
| Sceptical, high-consideration purchase | AIDA + strong proof (AIDCA) | Needs conviction |

You can also combine them — for example, a landing page that opens with PAS in the hero section and uses BAB in a case study.

### Step-by-step: from research to PAS or BAB

1. Pull the top three pains and outcomes from your message bank.
2. For PAS, pick the most frequently mentioned pain; for BAB, the most desired outcome.
3. Write the Problem or Before using verbatim customer phrases.
4. Write the Agitate or After with specific, honest detail.
5. Write the Solution or Bridge with the mechanism (how it works) plus proof.
6. End with one CTA.
7. Read it aloud and cut 20% of the words.

### Worked example: a courier service for small sellers in Pakistan

Research: sellers complain about late pickups and lost parcels during peak sales.

```
PAS version (ad):
"Late pickups again? During sale season every delayed parcel is an angry customer and a
bad review. Our scheduled pickups arrive in a two-hour window you choose, with live
tracking for you and your buyer. Book your first pickup ->"

BAB version (email):
"Before: refreshing the courier app and apologising to customers.
After: parcels collected on schedule, buyers tracking deliveries themselves, fewer
'where is my order?' messages.
Bridge: scheduled two-hour pickup windows plus automatic tracking links sent by SMS.
Set up your first pickup in five minutes ->"
```

Any service claims (two-hour window, tracking) must reflect actual operations.

### Before and after: the same product in PAS and BAB

Product (illustrative): an invoicing app for freelancers in the UAE and Pakistan.

```
PAS (for a problem-aware reader, e.g. a search ad landing page)
P  "Clients paying 60 days late?"
A  "Every chasing email feels awkward, and meanwhile your rent is due on the 1st."
S  "Send invoices with automatic reminders and card or bank payment links — most clients pay faster
    when paying takes one tap." (only claim 'faster' if your data shows it)

BAB (for an aspirational reader, e.g. a creator-led social video)
B  "Before: a spreadsheet of who owes you what, and a knot in your stomach every month-end."
A  "After: invoices go out in two clicks, reminders go out on their own, and you can see what's paid at a glance."
B  "The bridge: [App] — set it up in ten minutes with your first client."
```

### Agitate responsibly: a quick test

Before publishing PAS copy, check the agitation line against three questions:

1. **Is it true for this reader?** (Based on research, not imagination.)
2. **Is it proportionate?** No catastrophising, shaming or fear about health, safety or finances beyond the evidence.
3. **Does the solution genuinely resolve it?** If not, you have created anxiety you cannot relieve.

Regulators and platforms pay particular attention to fear-based copy for health, finance, children and vulnerable people. The UK CAP Code, for example, says marketing must not cause fear or distress without justifiable reason.

### Hands-on: generate both frameworks, then choose with evidence

```text
Product: [..]. Audience: [..]. Awareness: [..].
Pains (verbatim): [..]. Desired outcomes (verbatim): [..]. Proof: [..].
Write one PAS version and one BAB version, each under 80 words.
Agitate using only the listed pains; do not exaggerate consequences.
Then tell me which reader and channel each version suits, in one sentence each.
```

Run both as ad variations or email subject/body tests where you have enough volume; otherwise pick by awareness level and channel.

### Common mistakes

- Over-agitating to the point of fear-mongering.
- Vague problems ("growing your business is hard") instead of specific ones.
- An After state that is unrealistic or unsupported.
- Forgetting the bridge — describing the transformation without explaining how.
- Using PAS for a reader who is not aware of the problem yet.
keyTakeaways: PAS starts with a recognised problem; BAB leads with the desired transformation.
Agitate honestly and proportionately — never fear-monger or shame.
Choose the framework based on the reader's state and the message's length.
Every bridge or solution needs a clear mechanism and supportable claims.

An aspirational reader for whom the product enables a positive change
knowledgeCheck.explanation: BAB paints a before-and-after transformation, suiting aspirational readers.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does 'agitate responsibly' mean?
options: Help the reader feel the real cost of the problem without inventing or inflating consequences
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Truthful, proportionate agitation respects readers and complies with advertising rules.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which agitation line is most appropriate for PAS copy aimed at freelancers who struggle with late payments?
options: 'Late payments will ruin your life and your family will suffer'
'Every chasing email feels awkward — and meanwhile your rent is still due on the 1st'
'Nine out of ten freelancers go bankrupt from late invoices' (no source)
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Good agitation is true for the reader, proportionate and resolvable by the product. The other options catastrophise, shame, or use an unsupported statistic.

scenes.narration: Some readers are running away from a problem. Others are running towards a dream. The same product can serve both, but the copy that moves each of them is different. That's what PAS and BAB are for. PAS stands for problem, agitate, solution. BAB stands for before, after, bridge. In this lecture you'll learn when to use each, how to agitate a problem without crossing into fearmongering, and how to write both versions for the same product. Then you'll watch me generate both with AI and choose between them with evidence, not gut feeling.

scenes.narration: Why have two frameworks? Because motivation comes in two flavours. Some people act to avoid pain. My clients pay late, and it's stressing me out. Others act to gain something. I want to look like a proper agency to big clients. Research tells you which flavour dominates for your audience and channel. Someone typing a problem into a search engine is usually problem-aware and running from pain, so PAS fits. Someone scrolling a creator's video is often more open to aspiration, so BAB fits. The framework follows the reader's state of mind.
scenes.onScreen:
Two flavours of motivation
• Avoid pain → PAS
• Gain something → BAB
• Search is often pain; social often aspiration
scenes.visual: Layout: a two-column table builds: 'avoid pain' with a search bar icon, 'gain' with a phone feed icon. Example quotes from customers drop into each column. Timing (40s): title 0-3s; 3 bullets build in narration order about every 11s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Let's start with PAS. Problem: name the problem in the reader's own words, so they feel recognised. Agitate: explore the consequences, what it costs them in time, money, stress or missed opportunities. Solution: introduce your product as the way out, with proof. Think of a good doctor. They name what's going on, they explain honestly why it matters if you ignore it, and then they prescribe the treatment. The key word is honestly. A good doctor doesn't scare you into a treatment you don't need.
scenes.onScreen:
PAS: problem, agitate, solution
• Problem in the reader's words
• Agitate: real consequences
• Solution: the way out, with proof
scenes.visual: Layout: three stacked cards labelled P, A, S slide in one after another; a doctor's clipboard icon sits beside them, with the word 'honestly' underlined at the end. Timing (37s): title 0-3s; 3 bullets build in narration order about every 10s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Agitation is where copy goes wrong. Here's a simple test before you publish. First, is it true for this reader, based on research, not imagination? Second, is it proportionate, with no catastrophising, shaming, or fear about health, money or safety beyond the evidence? Third, does your solution genuinely resolve it? If not, you've created anxiety you can't relieve. Regulators take this seriously. The UK advertising code, for example, says marketing shouldn't cause fear or distress without good reason. And ad platforms restrict fear-based copy in areas like health and finance.
scenes.onScreen:
Agitate responsibly
• True for this reader?
• Proportionate, no shaming?
• Does the solution really resolve it?
scenes.visual: Layout: a three-gate checklist; a draft agitation line passes through each gate. At gate two it gets a red flag for exaggeration, is rewritten, and passes all three with green ticks. Timing (39s): title 0-3s; 3 bullets build in narration order about every 10s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Now BAB. Before: describe the reader's current world. After: paint the world once the problem is solved. Bridge: show how your product gets them from before to after. BAB works brilliantly for transformations, like fitness, education, software that saves time, or services that change how someone works. Picture a renovation show. You see the cramped old kitchen. You see the bright new one. Then they show you how it was done. The contrast creates desire, and the bridge makes it feel achievable.
scenes.onScreen:
BAB: before, after, bridge
• Before: their current world
• After: the problem solved
• Bridge: how your product gets them there

Timing (36s): title 0-3s; 3 bullets build in narration order about every 9s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: A simple example with both frameworks, for an invoicing app for freelancers in the UAE and Pakistan. PAS for a search landing page. Problem: clients paying sixty days late? Agitate: every chasing email feels awkward, and meanwhile your rent is due on the first. Solution: send invoices with automatic reminders and one-tap payment links. BAB for a creator video. Before: a spreadsheet of who owes you what, and a knot in your stomach every month-end. After: invoices go out in two clicks, reminders go on their own, and you see what's paid at a glance. Bridge: set it up in ten minutes with your first client.

• BAB: spreadsheet stress → paid at a glance → 10-minute setup

scenes.narration: A quick word on AI and these frameworks. Language models love PAS, and they love to agitate. Ask for problem-agitate-solution copy without guardrails and you'll often get dramatic lines about ruined weekends, lost fortunes and sleepless nights. That's not persuasion, it's melodrama, and in sensitive categories it can breach advertising rules. So give the model your real pains, in customers' words, and tell it explicitly not to exaggerate consequences. Then read the agitation line out loud. If you'd feel awkward saying it to a customer's face, rewrite it. The same goes for BAB: models tend to make the after impossibly perfect. Ask for an after that a real customer has actually described.
scenes.onScreen:
AI and PAS/BAB
• Models over-agitate by default
• Supply real pains; forbid exaggeration
• Read it aloud: would you say it face to face?

scenes.narration: Now a realistic business scenario, with illustrative details. A courier service in Pakistan serves small online sellers. Their research shows two distinct groups. Group one has been burned: parcels lost, cash-on-delivery payments delayed for weeks. They're running from pain. Group two is new sellers who dream of scaling from Instagram to their own store. For group one, the team writes PAS for search ads and a comparison page: tired of waiting weeks for your COD money? Then the agitation, delayed cash means you can't restock before the sale. Then the solution, with a clear settlement schedule they can honour. For group two, BAB in creator partnerships: from packing orders at the kitchen table to a proper shipping setup. Two frameworks, two segments, two channels.

Realistic example: Pakistani courier (illustrative)

• New sellers → BAB via creators

scenes.narration: Watch me generate both and choose. I give my assistant the product, the audience and awareness level, the pains and desired outcomes in customers' exact words, and my list of proof. I ask for one PAS version and one BAB version, each under eighty words, and I tell it to agitate using only the listed pains, without exaggerating consequences. Then I ask which reader and channel each version suits. Now my part. I check the agitation line against the three questions: true, proportionate, resolvable. If I have enough traffic, I run both as ad variations. If not, I choose by awareness level and channel, and write down why, so we can revisit it later.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me do it: PAS vs BAB with AI
• 1 Feed pains, outcomes, proof
• 2 One of each, under 80 words
• 3 Run the agitation test
• 4 Test both or choose by awareness

Two outputs appear side by side; the three-gate checklist animates over the PAS version; a decision note card is written at the end. Timing (50s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 10s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: How do you choose when you can't test? Use this quick guide. Problem-aware readers who search for a fix: PAS. Aspirational or unaware readers in feeds: BAB, often told as a story. High-stakes, anxious categories like health or finance: lean towards BAB or a gentle PAS, because heavy agitation can feel manipulative. Retargeting people who already know you: neither needs much agitation, so focus on proof and offer. And remember, these frameworks can nest. A landing page might open with BAB in the hero, then use PAS in the section that handles the most common objection.
scenes.onScreen:
Choosing between them
• Searching for a fix → PAS
• Scrolling, aspirational → BAB
• Sensitive categories → gentle
• They can nest on one page
scenes.visual: Layout: a simple decision tree builds top-down with four branches ending in PAS, BAB, gentle PAS/BAB and 'proof + offer'. A landing page thumbnail then shows BAB in the hero and PAS lower down. Timing (42s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 8s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Agitating a problem the reader doesn't actually have. Over-agitating until the copy feels manipulative. Making the after in BAB so perfect that nobody believes it. Forgetting the bridge, so readers see the dream but not how your product gets them there. And using these frameworks as templates, filling in the blanks with generic phrases instead of research. The frameworks give you structure. Your message bank gives you the words.
scenes.onScreen:
Common mistakes
• Agitating a problem they don't have
• Over-agitation
• An 'after' too perfect to believe
• A missing bridge

scenes.narration: Recap. PAS suits readers running from a problem: name it, agitate honestly, then solve it with proof. BAB suits readers running towards a dream: show before, after, and the bridge. Agitation must be true, proportionate and resolvable. Choose the framework by awareness and channel, test both when you can, and fill them with customers' own words. Try this now: write a PAS and a BAB version for one product you know, under eighty words each, and run the agitation test on the PAS version. The lesson text includes both examples side by side and the prompt I used.

lessons.title: Proof, credibility and objection handling
lessons.body:
### Claims need evidence

Every persuasive framework eventually asks the reader to believe something. **Proof** is what makes belief rational. Without it, even the best-written copy sounds like marketing.

### Types of proof

| Proof type | Examples | Strength tips |
|---|---|---|
| Testimonials | Customer quotes, video reviews | Specific results and context; real names with permission |
| Case studies | Before, approach, after with details | Include numbers that are accurate and representative |
| Ratings and reviews | Star ratings from independent platforms | Link or cite the platform; never fabricate |
| Social proof | Number of customers, community size | Only if accurate and current |
| Authority | Certifications, awards, qualifications, media mentions | Must be real and relevant |
| Demonstration | Product videos, live demos, free samples, trials | Show, don't tell |
| Data | Test results, performance figures | Cite method and source; avoid cherry-picking |
| Guarantees | Refunds, warranties | Clear terms, honoured consistently |

### Making testimonials work

Weak testimonial: *"Great service, highly recommend!"*

Strong testimonial: *"I was spending every Sunday on invoices. Now it takes me 20 minutes on Friday and clients pay faster. — Omar, freelance developer, Dubai"*

The strong version names the **before**, the **after**, and the **person** (with context that helps readers identify). To collect testimonials like this, ask specific questions: "What was it like before? What changed? What would you tell someone considering it?"

### Rules for endorsements and reviews

- **Never fabricate** testimonials or reviews, or write them yourself on customers' behalf. Fake reviews are illegal in many jurisdictions; for example, the US FTC's rule on fake reviews and testimonials (in effect from late 2024) and the UK's Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 both target fake reviews.
- **Disclose material connections**: if a reviewer received payment, free products or commissions, that must be clear. Influencer content needs clear labels such as "#ad" or platform paid-partnership tools, following rules such as the ASA/CAP guidance in the UK and FTC Endorsement Guides in the US, and local regulators' requirements in the UAE and elsewhere.
- **Results must be representative.** If you show an exceptional result, clarify what typical results look like.
- **Do not selectively edit** reviews to change their meaning.

### Objection handling

Objections are reasons the reader hesitates. Common categories:

```
Price:     "It's too expensive" / "I can get it cheaper"
Trust:     "Is this company legitimate?"
Fit:       "Will it work for someone like me?"
Effort:    "It sounds complicated to set up"
Timing:    "Not now"
Risk:      "What if it doesn't work?"
```

Handle objections **where they arise** — near the price, near the CTA, in the product description — not only in a distant FAQ.

### An objection-handling matrix

```
| Objection (from research)          | Where it arises | Response in copy                              | Proof                        |
|------------------------------------|-----------------|-----------------------------------------------|------------------------------|
| "Too expensive for a small shop"   | Pricing         | Cost vs time saved; monthly option            | Case study of similar shop   |
| "Setup looks complicated"          | Hero, features  | "Set up in 10 minutes — we'll help you"       | Setup video, support hours   |
| "Will customers trust the link?"   | How it works    | Show the customer-facing screen               | Recognised payment logos      |
| "What if I want to leave?"         | Near CTA        | "Cancel any time, export your data"           | Clear cancellation page       |
```

### Worked example: an online Quran and Arabic academy

Research with parents in the UK and US reveals objections: teacher qualifications, child safety online, and scheduling across time zones. The page adds:

- A teacher profiles section with verified qualifications and background-check policy.
- A "Safety first" section: parents can join lessons, sessions are recorded with consent, clear safeguarding contact.
- A scheduling widget showing available slots in the parent's local time.
- Testimonials from parents (with permission) naming the concern they had before and how it was addressed.

### The review and endorsement rules now in force

Proof is the area of copywriting where regulation has tightened most:

- **United States** — the FTC's *Trade Regulation Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials* (16 CFR Part 465, effective 21 October 2024) prohibits fake or false reviews and testimonials (explicitly including AI-generated fake reviews), buying positive or negative reviews, conditioning incentives on a review's sentiment, suppressing negative reviews, company-controlled "independent" review sites, and certain undisclosed insider reviews. The FTC can seek civil penalties. The FTC's Endorsement Guides (updated 2023) still govern disclosure of material connections.
- **United Kingdom** — under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024, from 6 April 2025 submitting or commissioning fake reviews, and publishing reviews in a misleading way (for example hiding negative ones or not disclosing incentivised reviews), are banned practices. The CMA can fine directly, up to 10% of global turnover.
- **EU** — the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (as amended by the Omnibus Directive) requires traders who show reviews to say whether and how they check that reviews come from real customers.
- **Gulf and Pakistan** — consumer protection and e-commerce laws prohibit misleading information; platforms such as Amazon, noon and Daraz also enforce their own review policies.

Practical rules for copywriters: quote real customers with permission, keep the source on file, show typical rather than exceptional results (or clearly say the result is not typical — in the US, the Endorsement Guides expect the generally expected result to be disclosed), disclose any incentive, and never write "customer" quotes yourself — or ask an AI to.

### Hands-on: a proof inventory

```
| Claim on page | Proof type | Source/file | Permission? | Last verified | Typical result? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| "Setup in 10 minutes" | Product demo video + median onboarding time | analytics export 2026-08 | n/a | 2026-09 | yes (median) |
| Testimonial: "paid in 3 days" | Customer quote | signed consent form | yes | 2026-06 | no - label as individual experience |
```

Review this table quarterly. Remove any proof that is out of date (old ratings, expired awards, clients who have left).

### Before and after: objection handling in an FAQ

```
BEFORE  Q: "Is it safe?"  A: "Yes, we take security very seriously."
AFTER   Q: "Is my card data safe?"
        A: "We never see or store your full card number. Payments are processed by [payment provider],
            which is PCI DSS certified. You'll also get a confirmation SMS for every payment."
```

The "after" answer is specific, verifiable and names the mechanism.

### Common mistakes

- Generic testimonials with no detail.
- Proof hidden at the bottom of the page.
- Unverifiable claims ("award-winning" without naming the award).
- Ignoring objections because they feel negative.
- Undisclosed incentives for reviews.

### Collecting proof systematically

Build proof collection into operations rather than scrambling before a launch. Send a short request after a successful delivery or project milestone, ask the specific before-and-after questions described above, record permission to publish in writing, and store approved testimonials in a shared library tagged by product, segment and objection addressed. When you write a new page, you can then pull the proof that answers that page's specific objections.
keyTakeaways: Proof turns claims into belief: testimonials, case studies, reviews, demonstrations and data.
Strong testimonials describe before, after and who the person is — with permission.
Fake reviews are illegal in many markets; disclose all material connections.
Handle objections where they arise, using research to identify them.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which testimonial is strongest?
options: 'I used to spend Sundays on invoices; now it takes 20 minutes on Friday.' — Omar, freelance developer, Dubai
knowledgeCheck.explanation: It describes a specific before and after and identifies the person.

knowledgeCheck.question: A brand gives influencers free products in exchange for reviews. What is required?
options: Clear disclosure of the material connection, such as #ad or a paid-partnership label
Nothing if they like the product
Only disclosure in the brand's terms
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Material connections must be clearly disclosed under advertising rules.

knowledgeCheck.question: Where should objection handling appear?
options: Near where the objection arises, such as by the price or CTA
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Answering doubts at the point they arise reduces hesitation.

knowledgeCheck.question: A UK brand offers customers a £5 voucher 'for every five-star review'. Why is this a problem?
options: It is fine because the voucher is small
Conditioning an incentive on positive sentiment distorts reviews; under UK law misleading or incentivised reviews that are not properly handled are banned practices
Vouchers can only be given in the US
It is only a problem if the reviews are written by AI
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Incentives tied to a positive rating produce misleading reviews. UK rules (DMCC Act, from April 2025) and the US FTC rule both target this. If you offer incentives at all, offer them for any honest review and disclose them.

scenes.narration: Every claim you make triggers a silent question in the reader's head. Says who? Proof is how you answer it. And objections are the quiet reasons people don't buy, even when they want to. In this lecture you'll learn the types of proof and when each works best, how to make testimonials believable and legal, the review rules that tightened in the US and the UK recently, and how to find and answer objections before they cost you the sale. Then you'll watch me turn a vague FAQ answer into one that actually builds trust.

Proof, credibility and objection handling
• Every claim triggers 'says who?'
• Types of proof

• Answering objections before they cost sales

scenes.narration: Why does proof matter so much online? Because the reader can't shake your hand, look you in the eye or touch the product. Trust has to be built from evidence on the page. And the bar keeps rising. People have seen fake reviews, inflated follower counts and AI-written testimonials. So vague reassurance like trusted by thousands no longer works. Specific, verifiable proof does. A named customer with a real result, a clear demonstration, an independent certification, a guarantee you actually honour.

• No handshake online

• Specific, verifiable proof wins

scenes.narration: Let's sort proof into types. Social proof: reviews, testimonials, case studies, customer numbers. Authority: credentials, certifications, awards, media mentions, expert endorsements. Demonstration: videos, screenshots, before-and-afters, free trials, samples. Data: test results, specifications, performance figures, with the source. And risk reversal: guarantees and returns, which are a form of proof because you're betting on yourself. Think of it like a court case. One witness is good. A witness, a document and a demonstration together are hard to argue with. Stack different types.

scenes.narration: Testimonials deserve special care. The best ones are specific: a real name and role, used with permission, a concrete situation and a concrete result. Compare great service, highly recommend, with, we cut our month-end close from five days to two, from a named finance manager. Place testimonials next to the claim they support, not in a lonely carousel at the bottom. Match the testimonial to the reader: a clinic owner trusts another clinic owner. And show typical experiences. If a result is exceptional, say so clearly.

scenes.narration: Now the rules, because they've tightened. In the US, the FTC's rule on consumer reviews and testimonials took effect in October twenty twenty-four. It bans fake reviews, including AI-generated ones, buying reviews, making incentives depend on positive sentiment, and suppressing negative reviews, and the FTC can seek civil penalties. In the UK, since April twenty twenty-five, the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act lists fake reviews and misleading review presentation as banned practices, and the CMA can fine directly. The EU requires traders to explain how they check reviews are genuine. Marketplaces enforce their own rules too. The simple rule for you: never write a customer quote yourself, and never ask an AI to.

scenes.narration: Now objections. These are the reasons people hesitate: price, trust, effort, timing, fit and risk. Your research tells you which ones matter most. The trick is to answer each objection at the point where it arises. Price worries appear near pricing, so answer them there. Trust worries appear near the form or checkout, so security and guarantees belong there. Fit worries, is this for someone like me, belong near the top. Think of a great salesperson who answers your question just as you're about to ask it.

scenes.narration: A simple example. A small online Quran and Arabic academy serves families in the UK and the Gulf. Research surfaces three objections. Will my child actually engage online? Are the teachers qualified? And what if the timing doesn't work with school? The page answers each at the right point. Near the top, a short sample-lesson video shows a real class, with parents' permission. Next to the teachers section, qualifications and a note that female teachers are available on request. Near the CTA, flexible scheduling across time zones and a free trial lesson. Three objections, three specific answers, each exactly where the worry appears.

scenes.narration: Where do objections come from? You have to go looking, because customers rarely volunteer them. Four good sources. Sales conversations, where objections are spoken out loud. Support and pre-sales chats, especially the questions people ask just before they buy. Exit or on-page surveys asking, what's stopping you from signing up today? And reviews, including competitors' reviews, where people explain what nearly stopped them. Put them in a simple matrix: the objection, how often it appears, where on the journey it shows up, and your best answer with the proof behind it. The top three objections deserve prominent answers. The rest can live in an FAQ, written in the same specific style.

Exit surveys show the top objection is trust with money: is my customers' card data safe? The FAQ answer says, yes, we take security very seriously. That reassures nobody. The team rewrites it: we never see or store your full card number, payments are processed by a named payment provider that's PCI DSS certified, and you get a confirmation for every payment. They move that answer next to the form, add a real merchant testimonial about security, and track form completion over the next month. Specific mechanisms beat adjectives.

Column three, where the source lives, the file, the export, the signed consent form. Column four, permission, yes or no. Column five, when it was last verified. And column six, is it a typical result? Let me fill two rows. Setup in ten minutes: proof is a demo video and our median onboarding time from analytics, verified last month, typical. scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Vague proof like trusted by thousands, with nothing behind it. Testimonials with no name or context, which readers assume are made up. Old proof, like a rating from three years ago or a client logo for a client who left. Cherry-picked results presented as typical. Incentivised reviews without disclosure. And objections answered with adjectives instead of mechanisms. Each of these either fails to persuade or creates legal risk. The fix is always the same: specific, current, permissioned, honest.

lessons.title: Landing page copy, section by section
lessons.body:
### One page, one job

A landing page should do one job for one audience: get them to take a single, clearly defined action. Copy is the backbone of that page. Designers make it beautiful and scannable; copy makes it persuasive.

### Write the copy before the design

Writing copy into an existing design often leads to cramming words into boxes that were never meant to hold the argument. Better: write a **copy-first wireframe** — a document with sections in order — and then design around it.

### The section-by-section structure

```
1. HERO
   Headline: main outcome for the specific reader
   Subheadline: how / for whom / key differentiator
   CTA + microcopy (e.g. "No card required")
   Proof snippet (rating, notable customers with permission)

2. PROBLEM ("Sound familiar?")
   3 pains in customer language

3. SOLUTION / HOW IT WORKS
   3 simple steps from start to result

4. BENEFITS
   3-6 benefit-led bullets, each with a supporting feature

5. PROOF
   Testimonials, case study, reviews, demo

6. OFFER
   What's included, price, bonuses, guarantee

7. OBJECTIONS / FAQ
   Top 5-8 questions from research

8. FINAL CTA
   Restate outcome + CTA + risk reversal
```

Not every page needs every section. A simple lead magnet page might be hero, three bullets, and a form. A high-price programme may need all eight and more.

### Length: as long as needed, as short as possible

Page length should match the **decision complexity** and the reader's awareness:

| Situation | Typical length |
|---|---|
| Free, low-commitment offer to warm audience | Short: hero, bullets, form |
| Paid product under a low price point | Medium: add proof, FAQ |
| High-price or high-risk decision, cold audience | Long: full structure, detailed proof, extensive FAQ |

The goal is not "short" or "long" — it is **complete without being padded**. Every section should answer a question the reader actually has.

### Writing scannable copy

Most visitors scan before reading. Help them:

- **Descriptive subheadings** that summarise the section ("Set up in 10 minutes", not "Simplicity").
- **Short paragraphs** — two to three sentences.
- **Bullet lists** for benefits and features.
- **Bold** a few key phrases (not whole paragraphs).
- **Front-load** sentences: put the important words first.

A useful test: read only the headline, subheadings and bold text. Does the page still make its argument?

### Worked example: a lead magnet page for an agency

A performance-marketing agency serving e-commerce brands in the UAE and Saudi Arabia offers a free guide.

```
HEADLINE:    "The 2026 Ramadan Ad Planning Checklist for Gulf E-commerce Brands"
SUBHEADLINE: "A 3-page checklist covering budgets, creative, timing and tracking —
              built from campaigns we've managed."
BULLETS:
- When to start creative production so ads are approved in time
- How to structure budgets across pre-Ramadan, Ramadan and Eid
- The tracking checks to run before spend increases
FORM:        First name, work email
CTA:         "Send me the checklist"
MICROCOPY:   "We'll email the PDF instantly. Unsubscribe any time. See our privacy policy."
```

The copy is specific about format, content and what happens next, and includes privacy information at the point of data collection.

### Legal essentials on landing pages

- Clear identity of the business (name, contact, where required by law, registration details).
- Privacy notice linked wherever personal data is collected.
- Marketing consent handled as required by applicable law (for example, unticked boxes where opt-in is needed).
- Prices, fees and terms clear.
- Disclaimers for results claims where appropriate.

### Hands-on: a copy-first landing page brief (Markdown you can hand to a designer or an AI page builder)

Many teams now draft pages in AI page builders (for example in Webflow, Framer, Wix, Shopify or WordPress) or ask a general AI assistant for a first layout. The output is only as good as the copy brief you give it. Write the copy first, in this structure, then let the tool lay it out:

```markdown
# Page goal: book a free 20-minute SEO audit call (one primary CTA)
Traffic source: Google search ads for "seo agency for dentists uk"
Reader: private dental clinic owner/manager, problem-aware

## Hero
H1: More new-patient bookings from Google — for private dental clinics
Sub: Local SEO and Google Ads run by a team that only works with dentists.
CTA: Book my free audit call | Microcopy: 20 minutes, no obligation, you keep the audit

## Proof strip
3 clinic logos (permission on file) | "Booked consultations up month on month" - Dr A. Khan, Leeds (verified quote)

## Problem → outcome (PAS)
...
## How it works (3 steps)
...
## FAQ (top 4 objections from sales calls)
...
## Final CTA block (repeat CTA + what happens next)
```

Review what the tool produces against the brief: AI layouts often add generic sections ("Our mission"), stock claims or extra CTAs. Delete anything that does not serve the page goal.

### Before and after: the first screen of a course landing page

```
BEFORE
H1  "Welcome to Digital Mastery Academy"
Sub "Unlock your potential with our world-class programmes."
CTA "Explore"

AFTER
H1  "Get your first freelance design client in 8 weeks"
Sub "A live cohort for beginners in Pakistan and the Gulf: portfolio reviews every week,
     client-pitch templates, and a certificate you can add to LinkedIn."
CTA "See the syllabus and dates"   Microcopy: "Next cohort starts 3 November. Pay in 2 instalments."
Proof "Past cohort projects" gallery (with permission) directly below
```

Note what changed: a concrete outcome and timeframe, a named audience, the mechanism (weekly reviews), and a CTA matched to the reader's awareness (see the syllabus before buying). Any outcome promise like "first client in 8 weeks" must be supported by representative results — if you lack them, rewrite as "Build a client-ready portfolio in 8 weeks".

### Measuring landing page copy

Track conversion rate to the primary action **by traffic source and device**, plus scroll depth and CTA clicks per section (via GA4 events or your analytics tool). If the hero CTA gets few clicks but the final CTA block converts well, readers need the middle of the page — do not shorten it blindly.

### Common mistakes

- Writing copy to fit a template design.
- Vague subheadings ("Our Approach") that do not summarise anything.
- Long paragraphs that nobody reads on mobile.
- Missing FAQs for known objections.
- Forgetting the final CTA after readers finish the page.

### Testing landing page copy

Once live, treat copy decisions as hypotheses. The elements that most often change results are the headline and subheadline, the offer and CTA, the order of sections, and how objections are handled. Change one major element at a time when possible, give tests enough traffic to be meaningful, and record what you learn about the audience — not only which version won.

### Landing page copy checklist

- [ ] Copy-first wireframe completed before design
- [ ] Hero answers what, who, why and what next
- [ ] Subheadings and bold text carry the argument on their own
- [ ] Proof and objections addressed with research evidence
- [ ] Final CTA with risk reversal
- [ ] Legal essentials present
keyTakeaways: Write a copy-first wireframe before designing the page.
Match page length to decision complexity: complete without padding.
Scannable copy uses descriptive subheadings, short paragraphs, bullets and front-loading.
Include privacy, pricing and identity essentials on every landing page.

scenes.narration: A landing page is a promise kept. Someone clicked an ad, an email or a search result because something promised them value. The landing page either keeps that promise in the first few seconds, or it loses them. In this lecture you'll learn the one-page-one-job principle, why the copy should come before the design, a section-by-section structure you can reuse, how long a page should really be, and how to write scannable copy. Then you'll watch me write a copy-first brief and hand it to an AI page builder, and fix what it gets wrong.

Every paid click, every email click, every social swipe lands somewhere. If that page is your generic homepage, full of navigation and competing messages, you're paying to confuse people. A dedicated landing page with one job focuses attention on one decision. It's like the difference between walking into a department store and walking up to a single, well-staffed counter for exactly the thing you came for.

Everything on the page either helps that action or gets removed. Principle two: write the copy before the design. When design comes first, words get squeezed into boxes that were drawn for a different story. When copy comes first, the design exists to present the argument. The designer, or the AI builder, gets a clear structure and knows what to emphasise.

Proof strip: logos, ratings or a short quote, right below the hero. Problem to outcome: a short section using PAS or BAB. How it works: three steps. Benefits: outcomes, each with a feature as proof. A free checklist download for a warm email subscriber can be a short page. A high-ticket consulting service for a cold audience needs more explanation, more proof and more objection handling. Short isn't automatically better. Readers who aren't convinced yet will scroll, as long as each section answers the next question in their head. Make it scannable with clear subheadings, short paragraphs, bullet lists and bold phrases that carry the message on their own.

lessons.title: Search ad copy: intent, relevance and constraints
lessons.body:
### Search ads answer a question

Someone typing into a search engine has told you what they want. Search ad copy should **reflect that intent** and show why your result is the best click. Unlike social ads, you are not interrupting — you are responding.

### Responsive search ads (RSAs)

On Google Ads, the standard text ad format is the **responsive search ad**. You provide up to **15 headlines (30 characters each)** and up to **4 descriptions (90 characters each)**, and the system tests combinations, showing up to three headlines and two descriptions at a time. Microsoft Advertising uses a similar format. Check current specifications before writing, as platforms update them.

Implications for copywriters:

- Each headline must **make sense on its own and in any combination**.
- Avoid repeating the same idea across many headlines — variety helps the system find good combinations.
- **Pinning** (fixing a headline to a position) gives control, for example for legal disclaimers or brand names, but reduces combinations — use sparingly.

### A headline mix for an RSA

| Role | Examples (for an online accounting course) |
|---|---|
| Keyword relevance | Online Accounting Course |
| Outcome | Get Job-Ready in 12 Weeks |
| Differentiator | Live Classes, Real Case Studies |
| Proof | 4.8/5 From Verified Learners (only if true) |
| Offer | Free Trial Lesson Available |
| Audience | For Career Changers & Graduates |
| CTA | Book Your Free Trial Today |
| Objection | Evening & Weekend Batches |

Descriptions expand the promise:

```
"Learn accounting with live classes and real business case studies. Evening batches available."
"Practical skills employers ask for. Book a free trial lesson and meet your tutor first."
```

### Message match and ad-to-page continuity

Search ads should lead to a page that continues the promise. If a headline says "Evening & Weekend Batches", the landing page should show the schedule prominently. Relevance between keyword, ad and landing page also influences ad quality assessments on search platforms.

### Using assets (extensions)

Search platforms let you add **assets** such as sitelinks, callouts, structured snippets, prices and images. Copy tips:

- **Sitelinks**: route intent — "Course Schedule", "Fees & Instalments", "Student Reviews".
- **Callouts**: short proof points — "Certified Tutors", "Instalment Plans", "Career Support".
- **Structured snippets**: lists under a header, for example Courses: Bookkeeping, Payroll, Tax Basics.

Assets increase the space your ad occupies and answer questions before the click.

### Policy essentials

Search platforms enforce editorial and content policies. Common issues:

- Excessive capitalisation or punctuation ("FREE!!!").
- Unverifiable superlatives ("Best in the world") — may require substantiation.
- Trademarks — restrictions vary; do not use competitor trademarks in ad text without understanding the rules.
- Restricted categories (financial services, healthcare, gambling, alcohol) that require certification or have country-specific rules.

### Worked example: an emergency plumber

Searchers typing "emergency plumber near me" want speed and reliability.

```
Headlines:
- Emergency Plumber in Leeds
- 24/7 Call-Outs, Local Engineers
- Upfront Prices Before We Start
- Gas Safe Registered Engineers   (only if true)
- Call Now — Fast Response
Descriptions:
- "Local plumbers available 24/7 for leaks, burst pipes and blocked drains. Upfront pricing."
- "Call now to speak to a real person. We'll give you an arrival window before we set off."
```

The copy prioritises urgency, trust and price transparency — the concerns of an emergency searcher.

### Search ads in the AI Max and Performance Max era

Google's automation increasingly writes and assembles search ads for you:

- **Responsive search ads (RSAs)** accept up to 15 headlines (30 characters) and 4 descriptions (90 characters) and combine them automatically — check the current limits in Google Ads Help.
- **Automatically created assets** and **AI Max for Search campaigns** can generate headlines and descriptions from your landing page and existing ads, and may adapt text to the query. **Performance Max** builds ads from your asset groups across Search, Shopping, YouTube, Display, Gmail, Maps and Discover.
- Microsoft Advertising offers similar responsive and automatically generated formats.

What this means for the copywriter: your **landing page copy becomes ad copy input**, so vague or non-compliant page text can surface in ads. Supply strong, specific assets; review generated assets in the asset report; remove any that misstate prices, delivery or claims; and use brand guidelines or exclusions where the platform supports them.

### Hands-on: build an RSA asset set in a spreadsheet (with a length checker)

Draft assets in a sheet so you can check lengths and coverage before uploading:

```python
headlines = [
    "Emergency Plumber in Leeds",      # keyword/location
    "Arrive Within 60 Minutes",         # only if operations can guarantee it
    "No Call-Out Fee Before 8pm",       # offer (verify terms)
    "Gas Safe Registered Engineers",    # proof (must be true)
    "Fixed Price Quote by Phone",        # objection handling
    "Call Now - Open 24/7",             # CTA
]
descriptions = [
    "Burst pipe or no hot water? Local engineers on call 24/7. Upfront price before we start.",
    "Gas Safe registered. Card, Apple Pay or bank transfer. Book online or call in seconds.",
]
for h in headlines:
    assert len(h) <= 30, f"Headline too long ({len(h)}): {h}"
for d in descriptions:
    assert len(d) <= 90, f"Description too long ({len(d)}): {d}"
print(f"{len(headlines)} headlines, {len(descriptions)} descriptions OK")
```

Aim for variety across angles (keyword, benefit, offer, proof, objection, CTA) so the system has genuinely different combinations to try. Character limits count every character, including spaces.

### Before and after

| Before | After |
|---|---|
| "Best Plumbers - Quality Service" | "Emergency Plumber in Leeds" + "Upfront Price Before We Start" |
| "Welcome to Our Website" | "Book a Boiler Service Online" |
| "Cheap Visa Services!!!" | "UK Visit Visa Application Help" + "Fixed Fee, No Hidden Charges" (only if accurate; avoid implying government affiliation) |

### Common mistakes

- Generic headlines that could apply to any competitor.
- Ignoring the searcher's intent (for example, selling features to someone searching for prices).
- Ten near-identical headlines.
- Promises the landing page does not deliver.
- Policy violations delaying approval.

### Keyword insertion and dynamic features

Search platforms offer features that insert the user's search term or location into ads automatically. They can raise relevance but may produce awkward or even non-compliant text if keywords are broad or include competitor trademarks. Use them deliberately, with sensible default text, and review how the final ads read. Always check the ad preview for each major keyword group before launch.

### RSA writing checklist

- [ ] At least 10 distinct headlines covering keyword, outcome, differentiator, proof, offer, CTA
- [ ] Each headline works in any combination
- [ ] Descriptions expand on benefits and include a CTA
- [ ] Assets written for top questions
- [ ] Claims verifiable and policy-compliant
keyTakeaways: Search ad copy responds to explicit intent — reflect it clearly.
Responsive search ads combine headlines (30 characters) and descriptions (90 characters); each must stand alone.
Use varied headline roles and assets to answer questions before the click.
Check editorial and restricted-category policies before launch.

knowledgeCheck.explanation: RSA headlines allow up to 30 characters; descriptions allow up to 90.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why must each RSA headline make sense on its own?

Only one headline is ever shown
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Headlines are assembled dynamically, so each must work independently.

knowledgeCheck.question: Someone searches 'emergency plumber near me'. What should the ad prioritise?

Speed, availability, trust and price transparency

knowledgeCheck.question: Your landing page says 'Delivery in 24 hours', but that is only true in two cities. Why is this now a bigger risk for search ads?

lessons.activity: Write a full responsive search ad (at least 10 headlines and 4 descriptions) plus four sitelinks for a service you know, and check each headline works alone.

scenes.narration: Search ads are the only ads where the customer tells you exactly what they want before you say a word. They type it. Emergency plumber Leeds. Best CRM for small agencies. Visa appointment help Dubai. Your job is simply to answer that question better than anyone else on the page, in about thirty characters at a time. In this lecture you'll learn how search intent shapes copy, how responsive search ads work, how to build a headline mix, why message match matters, and how Google's AI features now assemble and even generate ad text for you.

Search ad copy: intent, relevance, constraints
• The customer asks first
• Responsive search ads
• Building a headline mix
• Copy in the age of AI Max
scenes.visual: Layout: a search bar types 'emergency plumber leeds'; a results page fades in and one ad highlights. Bullets build on the right. Timing (42s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 8s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Why is search copy different? Because the reader is already in motion. Someone searching for an emergency plumber at eleven p.m. doesn't need to be persuaded that plumbing matters. They need to know you can come now, what it'll cost, and whether they can trust you. So search copy is less about grabbing attention and more about relevance and reassurance. Echo their query, answer their most urgent question, and remove the biggest worry. Clever wordplay has almost no place here. Clarity and speed win.
scenes.onScreen:
Why search copy is different
• The reader is already in motion
• Relevance and reassurance over attention
• Echo the query, answer the urgent question
scenes.visual: Layout: a night-time phone screen with a search query; three thought bubbles pop up: 'can you come now?', 'how much?', 'can I trust you?'. Each bubble is answered by an ad line. Timing (37s): title 0-3s; 3 bullets build in narration order about every 10s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Let's look at the format. A responsive search ad lets you write multiple headlines and descriptions. At the time of writing, Google allows up to fifteen headlines of thirty characters and four descriptions of ninety characters, but check the current limits. The system combines them automatically, testing combinations and showing the ones it predicts will perform best for each search. Think of it like giving a chef a well-stocked pantry instead of a fixed recipe. The better and more varied your ingredients, the better the dishes the system can make.
scenes.onScreen:
Responsive search ads
• Many headlines + descriptions
• The system assembles combinations
• Varied ingredients → better ads
scenes.visual: Layout: a pantry shelf of labelled jars, each a headline or description; a robotic arm picks different jars to assemble three different ad combinations on a counter. Timing (39s): title 0-3s; 3 bullets build in narration order about every 10s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: So what should your ingredients be? Build a headline mix across angles. Keyword and location: emergency plumber in Leeds. Benefit: arrive within sixty minutes, but only if operations can guarantee it. Offer: no call-out fee before eight p.m. Proof: Gas Safe registered engineers, which must be true. Objection handling: fixed-price quote by phone. And a call to action: call now, open twenty-four seven. Descriptions expand on the most important points in full sentences. Each headline must make sense on its own, because you don't control which ones appear together.
scenes.onScreen:
A headline mix
• Keyword + location
• Benefit and offer
• Proof and objection handling
• CTA — each one stands alone
scenes.visual: Layout: six headline tiles, each with a coloured angle tag (keyword, benefit, offer, proof, objection, CTA), drop into a grid. Two description bars slide in beneath. Timing (39s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 8s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Next, message match. The ad makes a promise, and the landing page must keep it immediately. If the ad says book a boiler service online, the page headline should say book a boiler service online, and the booking form should be right there. If the ad says fixed-price quotes, the page should show how pricing works. When the page doesn't match, people bounce, and Google's systems notice. Relevance between query, ad and landing page affects how your ads perform and what you pay.
scenes.onScreen:
Message match
• Query → ad → landing page
• The page keeps the ad's promise at once
• Mismatch hurts results and costs
scenes.visual: Layout: three linked boxes (query, ad, landing page) with the same phrase highlighted in each. The page box changes to a mismatched headline and the chain link turns red, then corrects to green. Timing (36s): title 0-3s; 3 bullets build in narration order about every 9s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: A simple example. A plumbing company in Leeds has an ad that reads: Best plumbers, quality service. Welcome to our website. It says nothing a searcher needs. The rewrite. Headlines: emergency plumber in Leeds; upfront price before we start; Gas Safe registered engineers; call now, open twenty-four seven. Description: burst pipe or no hot water? Local engineers on call around the clock, with the price agreed before we start. Every line answers one of the three questions in the searcher's head: can you come, how much, can I trust you.

scenes.narration: Now a realistic scenario with illustrative details. A visa consultancy in Dubai helps residents apply for UK visit visas. Their old ad shouts cheap visa services, with three exclamation marks. It attracts low-quality clicks and some complaints from people who thought they were on an official government site. The rewrite does three things. It states the service clearly: UK visit visa application help. It states a verified fixed fee with no hidden charges. And it avoids anything that implies government affiliation, which matters because platforms restrict ads that could mislead people about official services, and regulators take it seriously. They also add a line that the embassy's own fees are separate. Clicks may fall a little. Qualified enquiries and trust go up.

• No implied government affiliation
• State official fees separately

Illustrative tag. Timing (53s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 11s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Watch me build an asset set properly. I draft everything in a spreadsheet, or a few lines of Python, with a length check, because thirty characters includes spaces and it's easy to go over. I list six to fifteen headlines, each tagged with its angle, and check I have at least two for each important angle. Then two to four descriptions. The script flags any headline over thirty characters or description over ninety. One headline, no call-out fee before eight p.m. and weekends, is too long, so I trim it. Then I ask one more question for every line: can operations honour this, today? If not, it doesn't ship.
scenes.onScreen:
Watch me do it: asset set with a length check
• 1 Tag each headline by angle
• 2 Check coverage per angle
• 3 Script flags over-length lines
• 4 Can operations honour it today?
scenes.visual: Layout: screen-recording mock of a code editor with the short Python list; running it shows one assertion error in red for a long headline; the line is trimmed and the run turns green. Timing (47s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 10s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Now the modern twist. Google increasingly writes and assembles search ads for you. Automatically created assets can generate headlines and descriptions from your landing page. AI Max for Search campaigns can adapt text to the query. And Performance Max builds ads from asset groups across search, shopping, YouTube and more. What does that mean for you? Your landing page copy is now ad copy input. If your page says vague things, or overstates something, those words can show up in ads. So write the page carefully, supply strong assets, review generated assets in the reports, and remove anything that misstates prices, delivery or claims.
scenes.onScreen:
Search copy in the AI era
• Auto-created assets from your page
• AI Max adapts text to queries
• Performance Max assembles across channels
• Review and remove bad generated assets
scenes.visual: Layout: a landing page on the left sends arrows of text snippets into a box labelled 'platform AI', which outputs ad cards. One output card shows an overstated claim in red and a hand icon removes it. Timing (45s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 9s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Policy essentials. Every claim must be accurate and supported, especially superlatives like best or number one. Don't use excessive punctuation, gimmicky capitalisation or misleading phrasing. Sensitive categories like healthcare, financial services, gambling and government-related services have extra rules and sometimes certification requirements. Trademarks in ad text can be restricted. And the landing page must work, load quickly and match the ad. Policies change, so check the current advertising policies for Google and Microsoft before launching in a new category.
scenes.onScreen:
Policy essentials
• Substantiate superlatives
• No gimmicky punctuation or caps
• Sensitive categories have extra rules
• Check current policies
scenes.visual: Layout: a checklist card; each line ticks as narrated. A small warning triangle appears beside 'sensitive categories' with labels health, finance, gambling, government. Timing (34s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 6s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Common mistakes. Writing generic headlines that could belong to any competitor. Too little variety, so the system has nothing real to test. Headlines that only work as a pair. Promising delivery times or prices operations can't honour. Sending every ad group to the homepage. And ignoring asset and search terms reports, which tell you exactly what people typed and which angles earned clicks and conversions. That report is free customer research. Read it every week.
scenes.onScreen:
Common mistakes
• Generic, swappable headlines
• Too little variety
• Promises operations can't keep
• Ignoring search terms reports
scenes.visual: Layout: red cards appear in sequence; the final card shows a search terms report table with a highlighted row labelled 'free research'. Timing (33s): title 0-3s; 4 bullets build in narration order about every 6s; final 5s hold on the key line.

scenes.narration: Recap. Search readers tell you what they want, so answer that question fast and clearly. Build a varied mix of headlines across keyword, benefit, offer, proof, objection and CTA angles, each standing on its own. Match the landing page to the ad. Remember that platforms now generate and assemble ad text, so your page copy matters more than ever, and you must review what the machine produces. Try this now: pull your top search campaign, tag every headline by angle, find the missing angles, and write two new headlines for each gap, with a length check. The lesson text has the script and before-and-after examples.
